significance: Provides invaluable insights into the religious, social, and cultural life of Song Dynasty China through a vast collection of supernatural tales.
description: The *Yijian Zhi* (夷堅志), or *Records of Yijian*, is a monumental collection of over 420 chapters of supernatural tales and anecdotes compiled by Hong Mai (洪邁, 1123–1202) during the Southern Song Dynasty (1127–1279). This expansive work provides a rich tapestry of Chinese folklore, religious beliefs, and social customs of the time. The stories encompass a wide range of subjects, including encounters with ghosts, spirits, demons, and deities; karmic retribution; miraculous healings; and moral lessons. Hong Mai meticulously documented these narratives, often attributing them to specific individuals and locations, lending an air of authenticity to the fantastical events. The *Yijian Zhi* serves as a valuable primary source for understanding the cultural and spiritual landscape of Song Dynasty China, offering a glimpse into the everyday lives and beliefs of people from all social strata.
name: Yijian Zhi
author: Hong Mai (洪邁)

extendedContent.title: Origins & Mythology
extendedContent.content: Hong Mai, a scholar-official of the Southern Song Dynasty, compiled the *Yijian Zhi* over several decades, drawing upon a wide variety of sources, including oral accounts, written records, and personal experiences. The stories reflect the prevalent belief in the interconnectedness of the human and spirit worlds. Many tales revolve around the concept of karmic retribution, where good deeds are rewarded and evil actions are punished, often in unexpected and supernatural ways. The narratives also feature a diverse cast of mythological beings, including local deities, ghosts of the deceased, and various types of demons and spirits, each with their own unique characteristics and motivations. While not strictly a work of mythology itself, it acts as a repository for the myths and legends circulating at the time.

extendedContent.title: Role & Significance
extendedContent.content: The *Yijian Zhi* played a significant role in shaping popular perceptions of the supernatural in Song Dynasty China and beyond. It served as a vehicle for transmitting moral and ethical values, reinforcing the importance of filial piety, honesty, and compassion. The stories also offered a form of entertainment and escapism, allowing readers to vicariously experience the extraordinary and the uncanny. Furthermore, the *Yijian Zhi* provides valuable insights into the religious landscape of the time, reflecting the syncretic blend of Confucianism, Daoism, and Buddhism that characterized Song Dynasty society. The text's detailed accounts of rituals, beliefs, and practices offer a unique window into the spiritual lives of people from all walks of life.

extendedContent.title: Symbolism & Interpretation
extendedContent.content: The symbolism within the *Yijian Zhi* is rich and multifaceted. Ghosts and spirits often represent the unresolved anxieties and injustices of the living world, serving as reminders of the consequences of immoral behavior. Miracles and divine interventions symbolize the power of faith and the potential for redemption. The recurring theme of karmic retribution underscores the importance of ethical conduct and the belief that actions have consequences, both in this life and beyond. The stories also reflect the social hierarchies and power dynamics of Song Dynasty society, often portraying the struggles of ordinary people against corrupt officials and supernatural forces. The *Yijian Zhi* can be interpreted as a reflection of the anxieties, hopes, and beliefs of a society grappling with political instability, social change, and the enduring mysteries of the universe.

extendedContent.title: Legacy & Influence
extendedContent.content: The *Yijian Zhi* has had a lasting influence on Chinese literature, folklore, and popular culture. It has served as a source of inspiration for countless writers, artists, and filmmakers, who have adapted and reinterpreted its stories for new audiences. The text's detailed descriptions of supernatural phenomena have also contributed to the development of Chinese ghost stories and fantasy literature. The *Yijian Zhi* continues to be studied by scholars of Chinese history, literature, and religion, who recognize its value as a primary source for understanding the cultural and spiritual landscape of Song Dynasty China. Its enduring popularity testifies to the enduring appeal of its tales of the supernatural, the power of karma, and the enduring human quest for meaning and understanding.
